*   **Divergence:** On GPUs, divergent execution occurs when some threads in a warp terminate early while others continue [S36, unofficial][S44, unofficial].

The claim states that divergent execution on GPUs occurs when some threads in a warp terminate early while others continue. Source [S36] explicitly mentions that 'divergent code paths are costly' in the context of GPU implementations where a conditional check (early ray termination) might cause some threads to stop (loop aborted) while others continue. Source [S44] confirms that early loop exit (termination) is implemented by breaking out of the loop and notes that this is not always optimal on modern GPUs due to 'divergent execution'. Together, the sources support the mechanism described in the claim: early termination by some threads creates divergence relative to those that continue.

The evidence explicitly states that the optimization (adaptive termination based on opacity threshold) works best for 'scenes with opaque or semitransparent surfaces where voxels away from surfaces have an opacity of zero' and that for such scenes, 'savings of up to an order of magnitude' (significant speedup) have been observed.

*   Performance gains are highly variable; for semi-transparent volumes with low depth complexity, ERT may provide no benefit and even incur a 30% penalty due to conditional overhead [S36, unofficial].

The claim states that performance gains are highly variable, ERT may provide no benefit for semi-transparent volumes with low depth complexity, and it can incur a 30% penalty due to conditional overhead. The evidence explicitly supports all these points: 1) It states 'the effects of ERT are highly variable'. 2) It cites earlier work [22] where 'a semi-transparent volume exhibited no improvement in runtime from ERT and instead sustained a 30% penalty from the additional conditional overhead'. While the evidence attributes the 30% penalty specifically to the semi-transparent volume case in prior work rather than explicitly linking 'low depth complexity' to that specific 30% figure in the current study's data, the claim's core assertion regarding the 30% penalty for semi-transparent volumes and the general variability is fully substantiated by the text provided.

Performance can degrade on highly transparent volumes due to branch divergence [S36, unofficial].

It further notes that in cases where ERT provides no reduction in steps, a 'penalty of 5% was measured.' This supports the claim that performance can degrade due to branch divergence (divergent code paths) in scenarios involving transparency (where the condition might not be met early, leading to divergence or overhead).
